options.option_text: Rs 6,000 per year (in 3 instalments) directly to small and marginal farmers
Free crop insurance
Subsidised fertilisers
Free seeds to all farmers

questions.explanation: PM-KISAN (2019): Rs 6,000/year (Rs 2,000 per 4-month instalment) to farmer families with up to 2 hectares of land. Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to bank accounts.

options.option_text: Health insurance cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year to poor families
Free medicines to all citizens
Rs 2 lakh accident insurance
Hospital construction grants

questions.explanation: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (2018): Rs 5 lakh/year health cover for ~10.74 crore families (bottom 40%). World's largest government-funded health insurance scheme.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council is chaired by:

options.option_text: Union Finance Minister
Prime Minister
President of India
Governor of RBI

questions.explanation: GST Council (Article 279A): chaired by Union Finance Minister. Members: state finance ministers. Takes decisions by three-fourths majority (Centre has one-third weighted vote).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) guarantees:

options.option_text: 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households
50 days of employment
Jobs in urban areas
Employment for urban youth

questions.explanation: MGNREGA (2005): guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual work per year to any rural household demanding it. Wages paid within 15 days (else compensation). Largest employment scheme globally.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Digital India programme was launched in:
questions.explanation: Digital India launched 1 July 2015. Three pillars: digital infrastructure, digital governance, digital literacy. Key initiatives: Aadhaar, UPI, CoWIN, DigiLocker, BharatNet.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme aims to:

options.option_text: Boost domestic manufacturing and attract investment by linking incentives to incremental production
Provide subsidies to agriculture
Give incentives to exporters only
Fund infrastructure projects

questions.explanation: PLI scheme (2020): incentivises companies to increase production/invest in India across 14 sectors (mobile phones, pharma, automobiles, textiles, etc.). Target: $520 billion manufacturing output.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What is India's long-term target for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions?
questions.explanation: India's NDC (Nationally Determined Contribution) to UNFCCC: achieve net-zero emissions by 2070. Interim: 50% power from non-fossil fuels and 45% reduction in emissions intensity by 2030.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Develop 100 cities with smart infrastructure, digital connectivity, and sustainable urban services
Build 100 new cities
Provide internet to all villages
Digitise land records in cities

questions.explanation: Smart Cities Mission (2015): 100 cities selected. Focus on integrated command and control centres, smart traffic, digital governance, waste management, and citizen services.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under PM MUDRA Yojana, the loan sub-category 'Tarun' covers credit limits in which range?

options.option_text: Up to ₹50,000 for first-time micro-enterprise borrowers
₹50,001 to ₹5 lakh for small businesses in the growth stage
₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh for enterprises seeking expansion capital
₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh for medium units needing working capital

questions.explanation: MUDRA's three sub-categories are Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishore (₹50,001–₹5 lakh), and Tarun (₹5 lakh–₹10 lakh). Option A describes Shishu; Option B describes Kishore. Option D is outside MUDRA's ambit entirely — loans above ₹10 lakh fall under regular MSME lending channels.

questions.stem: Under PMAY-U's Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS), which annual income band correctly defines the 'Middle Income Group-I' (MIG-I) category?

options.option_text: Annual household income up to ₹3 lakh (EWS category ceiling)
Annual household income between ₹3 lakh and ₹6 lakh (LIG ceiling)
Annual household income between ₹6 lakh and ₹12 lakh (MIG-I band)
Annual household income between ₹12 lakh and ₹18 lakh (MIG-II band)

questions.explanation: Under PMAY-U CLSS, MIG-I covers annual household income of ₹6–12 lakh. EWS is up to ₹3 lakh, LIG is ₹3–6 lakh, and MIG-II is ₹12–18 lakh. Option B (LIG) is the most common confusion since it is just below MIG-I. Examiners frequently test these income slab boundaries.

questions.stem: The Atal Pension Yojana (APY) offers a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹1,000–₹5,000 on reaching age 60. Which body is the nodal regulator and administrator of APY?

options.option_text: Life Insurance Corporation of India under IRDAI oversight framework
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)
Employee Provident Fund Organisation under the Ministry of Labour
National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)

questions.explanation: APY is administered by PFRDA through the National Pension System (NPS) architecture. LIC is a common wrong answer because it is associated with government-backed insurance; EPFO administers EPF and EPS but not APY; NABARD focuses on rural credit, not pension regulation.

questions.stem: Under PMGSY Phase-I (launched December 2000), all-weather road connectivity was mandated only for unconnected habitations in plain areas with a minimum population of?

options.option_text: 250 persons — the threshold applicable to hilly and tribal areas
500 persons — the standard norm for plain area habitations
1,000 persons — the earlier Rural Roads Plan minimum benchmark
750 persons — prescribed for semi-arid and desert region habitations

questions.explanation: PMGSY Phase-I set 500 persons as the minimum for plain area habitations and 250 persons for hilly, tribal, and desert areas. Option A (250) is the hilly/tribal threshold — the most commonly confused distractor. There is no 750-person or 1,000-person norm anywhere in the scheme guidelines.

questions.stem: The SVAMITVA scheme (launched April 2020) creates property cards for rural 'Abadi' land. Which primary technology platform enables its centimetre-level mapping accuracy?

options.option_text: LiDAR-equipped ground vehicles deployed by state revenue officials
Drone survey integrated with Continuous Operating Reference Stations (CORS)
Satellite imagery processed exclusively via ISRO's Bhuvan geoportal
GPS hand-held devices calibrated against Survey of India benchmarks

questions.explanation: SVAMITVA uses drone-based aerial surveying linked to CORS networks for centimetre-level positional accuracy, enabling legally defensible property cards (Rights of Record). Satellite imagery via Bhuvan and GPS hand-held devices lack the resolution for plot-level demarcation. LiDAR ground vehicles are not part of the scheme's methodology.

questions.stem: Under Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), the farmer's share of premium for Rabi food and oilseed crops is capped at?

options.option_text: 2% of sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is lower (Kharif cap)
1.5% of sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is lower (Rabi cap)
5% of sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is lower (commercial crops)
0.5% of sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is lower (pilot rate)

questions.explanation: PMFBY caps farmer premiums at: Kharif crops — 2%, Rabi food/oilseed crops — 1.5%, and annual commercial/horticultural crops — 5% (or actuarial rate if lower). The 2% vs 1.5% distinction between Kharif and Rabi is a classic PYQ trap. The balance premium above these caps is shared equally by the Centre and the State government.

questions.stem: Jal Jeevan Mission prescribes a minimum quantity standard for Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs). Which combination of water supply norm and the mission's original completion year is correct?

options.option_text: 40 litres per capita per day (LPCD) with completion target of 2022
55 litres per capita per day (LPCD) with completion target of 2024
70 litres per capita per day (LPCD) aligned to WHO drinking-water norms
55 litres per capita per day (LPCD) with completion target of 2030

questions.explanation: JJM (launched August 2019) mandates 55 LPCD — the standard carried forward from the National Rural Drinking Water Programme — with the original 2024 completion target. Option A (40 LPCD) was the older Rajiv Gandhi Drinking Water Mission norm, a deliberate distractor. Option D uses the correct LPCD but wrong year (2030 is the SDG-6 universal water access target). Option C (70 LPCD) is the urban piped water standard, not JJM's rural benchmark.
